analysis.one_liner: Creates a Pacific Northwest old-growth forest reserve closed to logging while keeping timber sales going on surrounding federal forests and paying displaced timber workers and towns.
analysis.headline: The House Agriculture Committee approved and reported the bill in October 1992, but the full House never voted on it before that Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up an Old-Growth Forest Reserve on federal lands in California, Oregon, and Washington to protect ecologically significant old-growth forests and habitat for the northern spotted owl and other species. Timber harvesting in the reserve would be banned except for narrow safety, salvage, and thinning exceptions, and the land would be withdrawn from mining, mineral leasing, and geothermal development. Outside the reserve, it would set up an interim timber sale program on the remaining spotted-owl forests, and it would fund a large assistance package for timber workers and timber-dependent towns: retraining, extended unemployment and health benefits, relocation help, and higher payments to counties for schools and roads. It would also require revised forest plans within three years, create science advisory panels, and set up a special process for California's Sierra forests.
analysis.who_benefits: Three groups gain: (1) old-growth forests, spotted owls, and associated species, which get a protected reserve closed to timber sales with limited exceptions and withdrawn from mining and mineral leasing [S3]; (2) timber workers and timber-dependent communities, who get retraining, supplemental unemployment benefits, extended income and health insurance during training, job-search and relocation help, and community economic-diversification grants funded by a special six-year fund [S3]; and (3) county governments in owl-forest regions, which receive an increased share of national forest revenues for schools and roads [S3]. The timber industry also gains a defined interim timber sale program on non-reserve owl forests and a stated goal of a 'stable and predictable timber program' [S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Old-growth forests, timber workers, timber towns

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an Old-Growth Forest Reserve in California, Oregon, and Washington closed to timber sales, with exceptions only for public safety, insect or disease emergencies, salvage after catastrophe, and special watershed rules.
Withdraws reserve lands from disposition under public land laws and from mining, mineral leasing, and geothermal development.

Provides timber workers with retraining, supplemental unemployment benefits, extended income maintenance and health insurance during training, and job search and relocation expenses, through a Timber Economic Adjustment Commission funded by a six-year special treasury fund.

Gives timber-dependent communities grants to diversify their economies and reduces dependence on old-growth timber, and increases the share of national forest funds flowing to counties for schools and roads.

Requires completion or revision of forest management plans for the spotted-owl forests within three years, with defined public participation and citizen advisory boards, and sets up joint research and monitoring on old-growth ecosystems.

analysis.who_pays: The timber industry would get less federal old-growth timber than before, since a large reserve is closed to harvest; mining, mineral leasing, and geothermal developers would lose access to reserve lands; and taxpayers would fund the economic assistance program, county payments, research, forest fire research centers, and the Sierra forests committee. Timber sale contracts and special-use permits existing before enactment would be grandfathered and could continue [S3].

drawbacks.text: Logging would continue on non-reserve spotted-owl forests under an interim timber sale program during a multi-year planning period, so old-growth outside the reserve would keep being cut while long-term plans are developed.
The bill includes a grandfather clause allowing timber sale contracts and special-use permits issued before enactment to proceed unaffected, so previously approved logging would go forward.
The economic assistance program, county payments, research, and a six-year special fund all require federal appropriations, an ongoing cost to taxpayers on top of reduced federal timber revenue.

Management decisions hinge on advisory panels whose members are partly nominated by congressional committee chairs, adding political channels into what would otherwise be purely scientific agency planning.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a genuine compromise bill: it traded real, permanent protection for a large old-growth reserve and real money for displaced workers and towns against continued logging on the remaining owl forests during the transition. Its main weakness is the multi-year interim period, during which unreserved old-growth would keep falling, and the grandfather clause that lets existing contracts run out. It costs taxpayers significantly, but it pairs conservation with genuine worker assistance rather than leaving timber towns to absorb the cutbacks alone.

outcome.mechanism: The Agriculture Committee marked the bill up, amended it, and formally reported it to the House in October 1992, but no floor vote ever happened before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993, so the bill simply died.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 9, 1992 by Rep. de la Garza and referred jointly to the Agriculture and Interior and Insular Affairs committees.
The Department of the Interior submitted an unfavorable executive comment on the bill on May 19, 1992.
Subcommittees of both committees held markup sessions in May 1992, and the Agriculture Committee ordered the bill reported amended on June 18, 1992.
The bill was reported amended by the Agriculture Committee as H. Rept. 102-1039, Part I, on October 6, 1992.
No further House action appears in the record, and the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 without the bill reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because no law was enacted, timber operators kept harvesting under the rules then in effect and no new reserve protections, worker assistance, or county payments took effect; the northern spotted owl forests remained governed by existing plans and ongoing litigation through the end of the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber operators kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. E. (Kika) de la Garza
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, steered it through his committee's markup, and reported it amended to the House on October 6, 1992.

for.name: Original co-introducers (Reps. Miller of California, Jones of North Carolina, Vento, Volkmer, and Studds)
for.what_they_did: Joined as original co-introducers when the bill was filed on April 9, 1992.

for.name: Cosponsors (10 House Democrats, 1 House Republican)
for.what_they_did: Added their names to the bill during the 102nd Congress.

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources (Interior and Insular Affairs)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by joint referral, sent it to its National Parks subcommittee, and never reported it out.

against.name: Department of the Interior (Bush administration)
against.role: Executive branch agency with jurisdiction over BLM owl forests
against.what_they_did: Submitted an unfavorable executive comment on the bill on May 19, 1992.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote after it was reported in October 1992, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No recorded vote was ever taken, so support was never tested on the floor; the bill's sponsorship was 10 Democrats and 1 Republican, and the visible opposition came from a second committee, the executive branch, and Democratic leaders who never scheduled a vote.

industries.note: The bill would close a large reserve to logging, cutting off old-growth supply, but it also guarantees an interim timber sale program on non-reserve owl forests, salvage harvesting in the reserve, and grandfathering of existing sale contracts, aiming at a 'stable and predictable timber program.'

The bill creates a commission to pay retraining, extended unemployment and health benefits, and community economic-diversification grants funded by a six-year special fund, plus a hiring preference for displaced timber workers on federal restoration work.

industries.industry: County governments in spotted-owl forest regions
industries.note: Counties would receive an increased share of national forest revenue for schools and roads, cushioning the hit from reduced timber sales.

industries.industry: Mining, mineral leasing, and geothermal developers
industries.note: Reserve lands would be withdrawn from the mining laws, mineral leasing, and the Geothermal Steam Act, ending new access to those lands.
